articleTitle: The US military seems to be getting nervous about the launch supply crunch
summary: The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced conditional loan commitments of $150 million each to Stoke Space and Rocket Lab to expand launch capacity as SpaceX moves toward retiring its Falcon rocket program. The article describes rising military launch requirements, problems with United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, and uncertainty surrounding replacement launch vehicles.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: SpaceX plans to retire Falcon if Starship is fulfilling its promise. Rocket Lab says Neutron is scheduled to make its first launch next year and attributes its price increase from $55 million to $70 million per launch to a surge in bookings.
coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The article interprets Pentagon support for competing launch companies as suggesting defense officials view Falcon retirement as a potential national security risk. Space Systems Command forecasts up to 249 medium-to-heavy-lift launches through the early 2030s, more than double its expectation just two years ago, while Vulcan has been grounded twice in the last two years and competing launch vehicles remain in development.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: Since the 1990s, the Pentagon’s assured-access-to-space policy has supported at least two US rocket programs capable of launching national security satellites. Previous support included direct subsidies, development funding, and launch contracts at premium prices, providing technical and financial insight, schedule priority, and in some cases keeping providers in business.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: Both launch-company loans are conditional and subject to various financial, legal, technical, investment, due diligence, and other requirements; the article does not establish that these conditions have been satisfied.

SpaceX’s commercial Falcon 9 cutoff applies to launches after 2028, not an immediate end to government launches: the Space Force can place Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy orders through 2029, with actual launches extending through 2033.
Falcon’s eventual retirement is conditional on Starship fulfilling its promise.
Starship may eventually launch national security payloads, but SpaceX’s near-term priority is its own Starlink Internet satellites and Starmind orbital data centers.
Vulcan’s solid rocket booster problems have caused two groundings in the last two years and prompted transfers of several national security missions to SpaceX.

Eligibility to compete for national security launches does not establish operational readiness: among Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Impulse Space, only Blue Origin has flown a rocket that could meet Space Force requirements.
Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, and Relativity Space are developing medium- and heavy-lift launch vehicles; Impulse Space is working on in-space propulsion.
The stated debut sometime next year applies to Nova Pathfinder, not Nova Block 2.
Neutron’s first launch next year is a Rocket Lab schedule claim, and the article describes the vehicle as still-unproven.
Rocket Lab’s backlog of 117 launches includes both Neutron and Electron orders; it is not a Neutron-only backlog.

The article does not provide dimensions, payload capacities, flight durations, battery life, camera specifications, coverage areas, floor restrictions, subscription requirements, cloud dependencies, key-retention policies, or FCC approval statuses for the rockets.
